Indite

Indite is the iron-indium sulfide mineral species with ideal formula FeIn2S4. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list marks it approved and gives the year as 1967 s.p.; this special-procedure notation is not a numbered approval accession. Genkin and Murav'eva (1963) described natural grains in cassiterite-quartz ore from the Dzhalinda deposit, Little Khingan, in the Russian Far East. Reflected-light microscopy, quantitative microspectrographic analysis and powder X-ray diffraction support the identification. The diffraction comparison with previously synthesized FeIn2S4 supports a cubic spinel-type assignment; it is not a new single-crystal structure refinement of the natural material. The measured natural grains had variable, approximately determined iron-indium-sulfur proportions rather than uniformly ideal end-member stoichiometry. Nearly all observed indite grains were replaced to varying degrees by veinlets of the distinct indium hydroxide mineral dzhalindite. Natural and synthetic diffraction intensities also differ for the 311 reflection, which the authors retain in their structural comparison. The ideal species formula therefore does not establish purity of the analyzed grains or of the surrounding ore. The proposed later hydrothermal introduction of indite during quartz-associated replacement of cassiterite is a geological interpretation of textures and associations, not an experimentally demonstrated formation pathway. Cited laboratory synthesis conditions and separate heating experiments on dzhalindite are not natural indite formation conditions. This record denotes the mineral species, separately from elemental indium, synthetic FeIn2S4 materials and the mixed cassiterite ore. No microbial mechanism, extraction yield, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned by this identity and natural-specimen evidence.

Kernite

Kernite is the Na2B4O6(OH)2·3H2O mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1927 rather than a sequential approval identifier. It is distinct from elemental boron, the broad borates commodity and the separately hydrated borax and tincalconite species. Gatta et al. characterized a natural Kramer Deposit, California, museum specimen by chemical analyses, single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 293 K and neutron diffraction at 20 K, supporting monoclinic P21/c kernite. Their Table 3 reports the specimen-specific empirical formula Na1.99B3.99O6(OH)2·3.01H2O and 50.90 +/- 0.20 wt% B2O3. Water at 26.40 +/- 0.20 wt% was estimated by treating the mass loss on heating to 800 degrees C as water, rather than being a separately measured recovery product. Table 2 reports Li2O below 0.01 wt%, and Table 1 reports rare-earth oxide signals below its element-specific detection limits; these censored observations neither mean zero nor establish the composition of all kernite deposits. The neutron refinement and maximum-entropy analysis favor static positional disorder for two water-hydrogen populations in this specimen, refining the older X-ray model rather than defining another species. Proton tunneling was not completely excluded. The two temperature refinements retained the same general structure, an endpoint comparison rather than a continuously measured stability interval. This identity and crystal-chemistry record does not adopt the paper's general criticality language, proposed industrial applications or inferred natural formation conditions as demonstrated extraction, microbial activity or deployment.

Kornelite is a monoclinic ferric sulfate mineral, represented in the September 2026 IMA list as Fe(III)2(SO4)3(H2O)6·1.75H2O. Its additional channel water is variable; historical seven-water formulae are not exact hydration measurements for every specimen. This species is distinct from paracoquimbite, ferricopiapite and undifferentiated ferric-sulfate salts. The evidence below separates abiotic synthesis of a characterized crystalline product from provisional diffraction assignments in mixed bacterial-culture solids. Neither experiment establishes a recovered iron product from ore or waste, industrial deployment or a criticality designation.

Kozoite-(La)

Kozoite-(La) is the lanthanum-dominant orthorhombic rare-earth hydroxyl carbonate mineral with ideal formula La(CO3)(OH), approved as IMA 2002-054. It is distinct from elemental lanthanum, other kozoite species, hydroxylbastnäsite-(La) and commercial rare-earth feeds. The original Mitsukoshi, Japan material consists of minute crystals in spherical aggregates with concentric La-dominant and Nd-dominant zones. Four La-domain microprobe analyses have average La0.83 and Nd0.40 on a two-cation basis, with appreciable Ca0.43; this is not a chemically pure La end member. Carbon and hydrogen could not be measured in that intergrown material: the reported carbonate, hydroxyl and water contents were calculated from an ancylite-type formula, while infrared bands support carbonate and OH. The analytical total including calculated volatiles is 101.19 wt%. Powder diffraction gives Pmcn and a = 4.986(4), b = 8.513(6), c = 7.227(10) Å; no single-crystal analysis was possible. Nearly matching diffraction patterns of the La and Nd species require chemical discrimination. The mechanism below concerns separately synthesized La carbonate, not dissolution of the natural zoned specimen. These sources do not establish microbial causality, industrial deployment or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

IMA:2002-054
Kozoite-(Nd)

Kozoite-(Nd) is the neodymium-dominant orthorhombic rare-earth hydroxyl carbonate mineral with ideal formula Nd(CO3)(OH), approved as IMA 1998-063. It is distinct from elemental neodymium, kozoite-(La), hydroxylbastnäsite-(Nd) and commercial rare-earth feeds. The original Niikoba, Hizen-cho, Japan material consists of crystals smaller than 10 µm in an alkali olivine basalt cavity. Six-grain microprobe analyses show a mixed rare-earth composition, including Nd0.85 and La0.61 on a two-cation basis, rather than a pure Nd end member. Fluorine was not detected; no detection limit is supplied. Carbon and hydrogen were measured separately by triplicate elemental analysis using approximately 5 mg portions. Synchrotron powder diffraction and Rietveld refinement give Pmcn, a = 4.9829(1), b = 8.5188(2), c = 7.2570(2) Å and Z = 4. Hydrogen positions were not located, and the original study could not exclude a nearly orthorhombic monoclinic structure without suitable single crystals. The thermal experiment below concerns this natural mixed-REE material, not an isolated synthetic Nd end member. These sources do not establish microbial formation, industrial recovery or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

IMA:1998-063
Kukharenkoite-(Ce)

A barium-cerium fluorocarbonate mineral with the ideal IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula Ba2Ce(CO3)3F and approval identifier 1995-040. This record denotes the Ce-dominant mineral species, not kukharenkoite-(La), a carbonatite ore or its constituent elements. Zaitsev et al. (1996) described natural specimens from the Khibina and Vuorijarvi massifs in Russia and the Mont Saint-Hilaire and Saint-Amable massifs in Quebec. Their KH1 specimen has mean Ce2O3 of 15.30 wt% and La2O3 of 6.61 wt% across twelve microprobe analyses (Table 2); this is a mixed-rare-earth natural composition, not the ideal pure-Ce formula or a recovery measurement. CO2 was calculated from stoichiometry because insufficient material was available for direct determination. Small apparent La dominance in KH5 was explicitly considered inconclusive because of interference-correction uncertainty; it is not assigned to the La species here. Krivovichev et al. (1998) refined a natural KH1 crystal from manganoan ankerite carbonatite at 293(2) K in monoclinic P21/m, with R = 0.044 using 2296 observed reflections. The idealized Ba2Ce(CO3)3F structural model and fluorine-centered coordination describe that mixed-REE natural crystal; they do not constitute a mineral-formation or extraction experiment. The 1996 description reports solubility in hydrochloric acid with effervescence without specifying acid concentration, duration, temperature, solid loading or yield. No quantified leaching or isolated-product recovery is inferred. Its suggested equivalence to historical zhonghuacerite-(Ce) was tentative because original material was unavailable. Deposited observed and calculated structure factors cited by the 1998 paper were not acquired. No microbial mechanism, industrial deployment or dated criticality designation is asserted.

IMA:1995-040
Kuliokite-(Y)

A natural yttrium-bearing aluminium fluorosilicate mineral, with current IMA formula Y4Al(SiO4)2(OH)2F5 and approval 1984-064. The accepted primary characterization is a 2025 re-investigation of Ploskaya Mountain, Kola Peninsula, Russia, material from the type locality, not an assertion that the analysed crystals are the original holotype. Wavelength-dispersive microprobe analyses of three crystals, each averaging 4–7 spots, show variable Yb and other heavy rare-earth contents; water was calculated from structural data rather than measured directly. A single-crystal refinement at 293(2) K supports monoclinic Im symmetry, replacing the triclinic interpretation discussed in the paper. The model used mixed Y/Yb scattering curves with total occupancy constrained to one for each Y site; those occupancies are not separate direct assays of every lanthanide at each site. Its seven-coordinate Y2 site was interpreted as favouring heavier REEs relative to eight-coordinate Y1. This is a crystal-chemical interpretation of natural material, not a demonstrated separation or recovery process. Only one hydrogen position was located; the F3 hydroxyl/fluoride ratio was fixed during refinement. The studied sample's idealized (OH)2.5F4.5 composition differs from the current IMA end-member formula. Suggested fluorokuliokite and hydroxykuliokite species remain hypothetical in this study and are not aliases or new records. The 1986 original descriptions and the 1993 natural-alteration study are contextual citations within the 2025 paper, not independently acquired evidence here. No criticality-list designation, microbial mechanism, laboratory synthesis, extraction yield or industrial deployment is asserted.

Kurnakovite

Kurnakovite is the Mg[B3O3(OH)5](H2O)4·H2O mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1940. The year is not an approval identifier. Its triclinic P-1 structure distinguishes it from its monoclinic dimorph inderite. It is also distinct from elemental boron, the borates commodity and a mixed borate-bearing experimental precipitate. Gatta et al. characterized natural Kramer Deposit, California, material by wet chemistry and neutron diffraction at 293 and 20 K. The structural model contains Mg-bound water and an interstitial water molecule, with chains connected by hydrogen bonds. Its specimen-specific chemistry is not a resource-grade survey: the reported water content assumes furnace mass loss is entirely water, and minor measured silicon may reflect impurities rather than structural substitution. Criticality and microbial activity are not inherited from boron content.

Kutnohorite

Kutnohorite is the CaMn2+(CO3)2 mineral species listed by IMA-CNMNC in its September 2026 master list (PDF page 119). Its status is grandfathered; 1903 is the original-description year, not an IMA approval number. The Handbook of Mineralogy places it in the dolomite group and describes ordered calcium and manganese in approximately equal proportions, commonly with magnesium and ferrous-iron substitution. Its generalized formula Ca(Mn2+,Mg,Fe2+)(CO3)2 and natural-specimen analyses describe compositional variation around the IMA endmember, not an invariant manganese grade. The Handbook reports occurrence in deposits associated with manganese-bearing sediments and identifies analyzed material from Kutna Hora in the Czech Republic and Franklin, New Jersey. The spelling kutnahorite appears in a historical reference title; the accepted species name used here is kutnohorite. This mineral is distinct from the dolomite group as a whole, bulk manganese ore, elemental manganese and manganese oxalates. No microbial mechanism or criticality designation is assigned here.

Laforêtite

Laforêtite is the silver-indium sulfide mineral species AgInS2, listed as approved by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 under 1995-006. Meisser and colleagues' original description concerns tiny natural inclusions in a single galena specimen collected from the Montgros mine dumps in Haute-Loire, France. Reflected-light observations, eight electron-microprobe analyses on two grains, and in-situ X-ray diffraction support the mineral assignment. The diffraction measurement used a roughly 20 by 30 micrometre inclusion; galena reflections were removed, and preferred orientation limits comparison of intensities with the separate synthetic reference. The natural material was assigned to the tetragonal low-temperature AgInS2 form. The authors' laboratory synthesis produced a multiphase comparator, not a pure natural specimen or microbial product; synthetic hardness measurements and preparation temperatures are not natural-specimen measurements. This species is distinct from elemental indium, bulk mine waste, and manufactured AgInS2 polymorphs considered solely by chemical formula. The sampled inclusions establish neither a bulk resource grade nor an extraction yield. No microbial mechanism, industrial recovery claim, or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned.

(1985) characterized natural plates from oxidized copper ore at Britannia Mine, North Wales. Their measured mixed-REE composition gave the empirical cation terms Ce0.78La0.55Nd0.55Sm0.09Gd0.05Y0.04 on the reported 17-oxygen basis, with 7.96H2O; it is not a pure Ce end-member or an ore-grade measurement. Water was determined thermogravimetrically, carbon dioxide by CHN analysis and rare-earth composition by electron microprobe; sample deterioration limited analytical totals. Diffraction indicated orthorhombic Pbnb, a nonstandard setting of Pccn. Atencio et al. (1989) also found their historically labelled Bastnäs lanthanite specimen to be Ce-dominant. The mechanism below concerns separately synthesized Ce carbonate phases and does not establish microbial weathering of these natural specimens, industrial recovery or a dated criticality designation.

Their reassessment of published Curitiba analyses includes La-dominant and Nd-dominant specimens, so neither all Bastnäs material nor all Curitiba material can be assigned to this species solely from its locality. Lanthanite-(Nd)

Lanthanite-(Nd) is the neodymium-dominant lanthanite mineral, approved as IMA 1979-074, with ideal formula Nd2(CO3)3(H2O)6·2H2O, equivalently Nd2(CO3)3·8H2O. It is distinct from elemental neodymium, the lanthanite group and other rare-earth carbonate species. Morrison et al. (2013) characterized a natural specimen from Mitsukoshi, Saga Prefecture, Japan. Electron-microprobe results averaged over 23 analysis points gave a mixed rare-earth composition with Nd0.95La0.61Pr0.17Sm0.12Gd0.08Y0.04Eu0.03 per two rare-earth cations in the reported empirical formula; water was assigned by difference. This is specimen chemistry, not a pure neodymium end-member, ore grade or recovered-metal yield. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 296 K resolved an orthorhombic Pccn structure containing sheets of rare-earth coordination polyhedra and carbonate groups. All rare-earth elements were modeled as Nd because of their similar X-ray scattering, so this refinement does not determine their individual site distributions. Water hydrogen positions could not be assigned reliably and were excluded from refinement; the proposed hydrogen-bond connections rely on oxygen geometry and bond-valence interpretation. The original CIF and reflection downloads remain unverified despite access to the complete article and its rendered supplementary crystallographic information. This record establishes identity and characterization without asserting microbial formation, extraction performance, industrial deployment or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Larderellite

Larderellite is the ammonium borate mineral (NH4)B5O7(OH)2·H2O in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Its grandfathered status G and year 1854 describe its nomenclatural history, not a sequential approval identifier. It is distinct from other ammonium borates, a generic experimental ammonium salt, elemental boron and the borates commodity. Fastelli and colleagues characterized natural material from Larderello, Italy, by powder diffraction, reflectance spectroscopy and thermal analysis. Figure 1b's starting-sample diffraction fit reports 94.3% larderellite, 0.4% bassanite and 5.3% polyhalite. These are fitted phase fractions in a mixed specimen, not an independent chemical-purity assay. The study does not establish biological origin or microbial activity merely because the mineral contains ammonium, and no criticality designation is inherited from boron.

Laueite

Laueite is a grandfathered triclinic manganese-ferric phosphate mineral with IMA ideal formula Mn(II)Fe(III)2(PO4)2(OH)2(H2O)6·2H2O and historical year 1954 in the September 2026 list. It is distinct from stewartite and pseudolaueite, which have different framework arrangements, and from strunzite, which has a different water content. Moore (1965) determined the P-1 structure of a natural Palermo No. 1 Quarry, New Hampshire crystal; hydrogen positions were not located. Baur (1969) proposed Mn(III) substitution from earlier bond lengths, while acknowledging other substituents; this was an interpretation, not a direct oxidation-state assay or current species formula. Grey et al. (2025) demonstrated an epitaxial orientation of laueite on stewartite in a natural Hagendorf-Sud composite crystal by single-crystal diffraction and indexed faces. Its rhomb contained both minerals. The EDS-derived laueite metal composition Mn0.66Mg0.17Fe2.17, scaled to three metal atoms, differs from the simplified refined Mn/Mg site occupancy 0.93(2)/0.07; neither is the ideal species formula. The ferric assignment and adjusted hydroxyl/water proportions were inferred from bond-valence and charge-balance considerations. Deposited checks flag displacement parameters, missing hydrogen sites and formula/Z reporting differences, limiting detailed atomistic interpretation. Suggested solution changes and heterosite-assisted nucleation remain paragenetic hypotheses. No controlled transformation, microbial mechanism, recovery performance or inherited criticality designation is curated.

Lorenzenite

Lorenzenite is the sodium titanium silicate mineral with ideal formula Na2Ti2O3(Si2O6), equivalent to Na2Ti2Si2O9. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list gives grandfathered status G and original description year 1901, not an IMA approval number. Ramsayite is a historical name for the same species, not a separate material owner. Sundberg, Lehtinen and Kivekas (1987) refined a natural crystal from Helsinki museum specimen 4937, labelled from Lovozero on the Kola Peninsula. Their Pbcn model contains pyroxene-type silicate chains, distorted TiO6 octahedra and seven-coordinate sodium. The single-crystal refinement used 778 selected reflections from 1167 measured independent reflections and reported R=0.026. The chemistry cited for that specimen was from earlier work, not a new bulk assay in 1987. Historical cell-setting and oxygen-coordinate discrepancies are discussed in the original study. This identity record does not assert a dissolution, synthesis or microbial mechanism, a recovery yield, industrial use or criticality inherited from titanium.

Ludlamite

Ludlamite is the ferrous phosphate mineral with ideal formula Fe2+3(PO4)2(H2O)4, recorded as grandfathered in the September 2026 IMA list. It is a distinct mineral species from the three-water phosphoferrite and eight-water vivianite. Moore (1971) investigated natural ludlamite crystals from the Palermo number 1 mine in an abiotic heating comparison. The lower-temperature arms retained the starting powder pattern, whereas the 240 degrees C arm gave a ferric product with diffuse diffraction unrelated to the initial mineral. This observation does not identify a pure crystalline product or establish a general transformation temperature for all ludlamite specimens. The ludlamite and phosphoferrite observations curated in this corpus are different mineral arms of the same study, not independent replications. No microbial process, isolated-product recovery or constituent-derived criticality designation is asserted.

(1965) originally described mckelveyite from four subsurface core and trona-mine localities in the Eocene Wilkins Peak Member of the Green River Formation, Sweetwater County, Wyoming, USA, proposing the uranium-bearing trigonal P-3 formula Na1.9Ba4.0Ca1.1Sr0.2RE1.5U0.3(CO3)9·5H2O after recalculating wet-chemical analyses of massive and crystal-aggregate fractions for 18.0-20.7 wt% acid-insoluble impurities (organic matter, authigenic biotite, acmite, and quartz). Subsequent studies cited by Demartin et al. (2008) showed that type mckelveyite-(Y) is triclinic P1 (mckelveyite-(Y)-1A) with formula NaBa3(Ca,U)Y(CO3)6·3H2O. Demartin et al. (2008) solved the first complete crystal structure on a uranium-free monoclinic Cc polytype, mckelveyite-(Y)-2M (a = 15.8213(7), b = 9.1364(4), c = 13.7522(6) A, beta = 112.44(1) degrees, Z = 4, R = 0.0283 for 4454 reflections with I > 2sigma(I)), from hydrothermal carbonate veins at the Cava Fabi talc quarry, Val Malenco, Sondrio, Lombardy, Italy, where CO2 and H2O were derived from structure solution rather than direct gas analysis. Following IMA-CNMNC guidance, the monoclinic Alpine material is a polytype (mckelveyite-(Y)-2M) of the species rather than a separate mineral species. Distinct from mckelveyite-(Nd), donnayite-(Y), ewaldite, and elemental yttrium or rare earths; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or extraction yield is asserted.

The synthetic formula [(UO2)4O(OH)6]·5H2O is the same ideal stoichiometry on a four-uranium basis. No criticality, microbial activity or industrial recovery is inferred from these laboratory mineral transformations.

Metatorbernite

Metatorbernite is the copper uranyl phosphate mineral Cu(UO2)2(PO4)2(H2O)4·4H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, with grandfathered status G. The year 1916 is a historical description year, not a numbered IMA approval. Its ideal eight-water composition is distinct from twelve-water torbernite, arsenate metazeunerite, calcium meta-autunite, uranyl ions and elemental uranium or copper. Locock and Burns grew synthetic metatorbernite in copper-bearing silica gel at room temperature over three weeks and refined an epoxy-coated, merohedrally twinned crystal in P4/n. Its 88.3(6)% fitted copper-site occupancy and constrained hydrogen model are specimen-specific; proposed oxonium charge compensation was not directly established. The 2023 natural Cornwall crystal instead gave the preferred P4/nmm model with a smaller c repeat. These are source-specific structural models, not grounds to replace all specimens with one symmetry or transfer occupancy between them. Thermal behavior below is abiotic laboratory evidence; neither criticality nor microbial extraction, isolated-product recovery or industrial deployment is inferred.

Metatyuyamunite

Metatyuyamunite is the calcium uranyl vanadate mineral Ca(UO2)2(VO4)2·3H2O. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list recognizes it with grandfathered status G; 1954 is the original-description year, not an IMA approval accession. This mineral-species owner is distinct from tyuyamunite, carnotite, the broader carnotite group, elemental uranium or vanadium and the mixed sandstone used experimentally. Glasauer et al. (2022) identified metatyuyamunite, written meta- tyuyamunite in the paper, together with fritzscheite in the starting natural uranium-vanadium sandstone. After incubation with living Shewanella putrefaciens CN32, metatyuyamunite was still identified by X-ray diffraction in the final fine fraction together with K-carnotite. Figure 1b and sections 3.1 and 3.3 support presence in both assemblages; they do not quantify its surviving mass or prove that the same crystals persisted. Section 4.1 explicitly states that the two starting minerals could not be observed separately during incubation. Thus the mixed-ore vanadium reduction cannot be assigned specifically to metatyuyamunite, and residual detection does not demonstrate complete resistance to transformation. Section 3.2 names tyuyamunite as a carnotite precursor while the conclusion instead names fritzscheite; neither statement establishes a resolved phase-specific pathway. The shared laboratory experiment used 1.6 g of mixed sandstone in 80 mL defined medium with 10 mM sodium lactate and 1 mM phosphate, nitrogen degassing and autoclaving before inoculation, followed by an anoxic glovebox incubation extending to ten months. Treatments were in triplicate. These three mineral records refer to the same experiment, not independent replications. Bacteria-free solution controls were included, but do not isolate each phase's fate. The mixed-ore spectra support partial V reduction while U remained predominantly U(VI); results from the separate soluble-salt arm must not be transferred to this mineral. Dissolved U was low, rather than established to be exactly zero. Section 3.2 gives a V plateau time of 120 days while Figure 2 labels the time axes in hours, so no exact kinetic endpoint is adopted. The species identity and bounded mixed-assemblage occurrence are curated without a mineral-specific mechanism assertion. There is no supported pure-metatyuyamunite rate, recovered-product yield or industrial- deployment claim here. No criticality designation is inherited from its constituent elements.

The year 1937 is a historical description year, not a numbered IMA approval. Monazite-(Gd)

Monazite-(Gd) is the gadolinium-dominant monazite species with ideal formula Gd(PO4), approved as IMA 2022-055. It is distinct from elemental gadolinium, mixed rare-earth ores and tetragonal xenotime-(Gd), which shares its ideal formula. Ondrejka et al. (2023) characterized natural microscopic domains from the Zimna Voda quartz vein near Prakovce, Slovakia, using wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analysis, Raman spectroscopy and selected-area electron diffraction of a focused ion-beam lamella. These observations support monoclinic P21/n symmetry. The six analyses in Table 2 average 22.84 wt% Gd2O3 and contain substantial Sm and Nd; this is mixed mineral composition, not pure GdPO4, a bulk ore grade or a recovered gadolinium yield. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction was not performed because of crystal size. The unit-cell dimensions emphasized in the abstract and Table 3 are estimates from weighted synthetic end-members; they differ from the less precise electron-diffraction measurements. Density was calculated, while hardness and several other physical properties could not be determined. The proposed hydrothermal enrichment explanation is a geological interpretation, not a controlled formation or extraction experiment. This characterization does not establish microbial production, recovery performance, industrial deployment or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Monazite-(Sm) is the samarium-dominant monazite mineral species with ideal formula Sm(PO4), distinct from elemental samarium, hydrated samarium phosphates, other monazite species and mixed rare-earth ores. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list assigns approved status and number 2001-001. The original description instead prints 2000-001; the current authority is followed here while retaining that source discrepancy. Masau et al. (2002) characterized natural crystals from the Annie Claim #3 granitic pegmatite in southeastern Manitoba, Canada, by wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analysis, optical examination, single-crystal diffraction and Gandolfi powder diffraction. The diffraction data support monoclinic P21/n symmetry. The analyzed natural material contains substantial Gd, Ce, Th and Ca and is not a pure SmPO4 end-member. Table 1 reports 13.02 wt% Sm2O3 for the average of three grains used for physical, optical and crystal data; its 14.29 wt% maximum belongs to a different analysis, not one of those extracted grains. These are mineral oxide compositions, not a bulk ore grade or recovered samarium yield. Density and hardness could not be measured; the reported densities are calculated. Selective rare-earth complexation during pegmatite crystallization is a proposed geological explanation, not an experimentally demonstrated extraction or formation mechanism. This natural characterization does not establish microbial biomineralization, recovery performance, industrial deployment or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Montebrasite

Montebrasite is the hydroxyl-dominant lithium aluminium phosphate mineral with ideal formula LiAl(PO4)(OH), distinct from fluorine-dominant amblygonite. The September 2026 IMA list records grandfathered status and original-description year 1871. Groat2003 Methods (pages 197-199), Table 2 (page 198), Table 11 (page 206) and neutron/NMR figures establish the natural substituted series: the Dunton specimen has neutron-derived F/(F+OH)=0.04, whereas estimates for the near-boundary Tanco specimen differ by technique and are not treated as a pure endmember. Triclinic primitive P-1 and centered C-1 are alternative settings, not evidence for separate polymorphs. In the Shirose thesis, Figures 13-16 (printed pages 29-31, PDF pages 36-38) show co-oriented lacroixite patches and low-fluorine montebrasite in a natural host; Figure 12 (page 25, PDF page 32) shows secondary montebrasite veins without lacroixite. Section 5.3 and Figure 19 (pages 34-36) interpret an exsolution sequence, but do not reproduce that sequence by controlled synthesis. Figure 21 and Table 5 (pages 38 and 39) include gem-quality XS110 with no observed lacroixite, so the patch texture is not universal. Lithium and water in the thesis microprobe tables were calculated stoichiometrically. These are primary identity and natural-texture observations; no microbial mechanism, measured lithium extraction, isolated recovery yield or mineral criticality is asserted. The studies are also used in cmmmech:amblygonite and are not independent experiments for each owner; the ambiguous XN163 heating arm is not transferred here as a montebrasite-specific threshold.

It is distinct from potassium jarosite, ammoniojarosite, hydroniumjarosite and a mixed industrial jarosite residue. (2024), sampling in May 2010, identified natrojarosite and quartz in an inner crust associated with a cyanobacteria-containing mixed microbial mat beneath a gypsum-rich outer layer at Río Tinto, Spain. This is an association, without controlled evidence that the organisms precipitated or dissolved natrojarosite, without a verified cyanobacterial species or strain, and without an extraction or recovery measurement. Navajoite

Navajoite is a hydrated vanadium-iron oxide mineral with formula (V5+,Fe3+)10O24·12H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, which assigns grandfathered status G and original-description year 1954. That year is not a numbered IMA approval. The complete 1955 description characterized selected natural material from the Monument No. 2 mine, Apache County, Arizona, with residual impurities and uncertain partitioning of iron and reduced vanadium; its tentative V2O5·3H2O formula and indexing are historical interpretations. Evans and Hughes later reindexed powder/fiber diffraction from USNM 106900, whose type status they marked uncertain, using a C-centered cell with C2/m indexing. They attributed two extra lines to probable bokite and found that some other specimens labeled navajoite were bokite or mixtures. Their revised empirical formula was fitted to Sherwood's original 1955 chemical analysis, not a new independent assay, and the diffraction work did not solve the atomic structure. The earlier proposed natural oxidation of corvusite and storage-related water loss do not establish controlled transformation kinetics or a microbial mechanism. Navajoite is distinct from associated corvusite, bokite, elemental vanadium and mixed uranium-vanadium ore. These sources establish no isolated-product recovery or industrial deployment, and the mineral does not inherit vanadium's criticality designations.

Parauranophane

Parauranophane is the calcium uranyl silicate hydrate mineral Ca(UO2)2(SiO3OH)2(H2O)4·H2O listed by IMA in September 2026. It is the historical beta-uranophane or uranophane-beta, renamed by CNMNC in August 2022. Rn, 2022 s.p. denotes that nomenclature action, not a unique approval accession. The alpha polymorph is the separate species uranophane; identical ideal composition does not make their experiments interchangeable. Cesbron and colleagues characterized natural beta material from Nopal I, Sierra Peña Blanca, Chihuahua, Mexico, by morphology and powder X-ray diffraction, including a refined monoclinic cell with space group P21/a in the reported setting. Their synthesis campaign produced uranophane but no beta polymorph under the tested conditions; its stability field remained unresolved. No criticality, microbial activity, extraction yield or industrial deployment is inferred from these mineralogical studies.

Pascoite

Pascoite is a calcium decavanadate mineral with formula [Ca3(H2O)17]V5+10O28 in the September 2026 IMA list, which assigns grandfathered status G and original-description year 1914. That year is not a numbered IMA approval. Hughes and colleagues characterized a natural crystal from Harvard specimen 91449, Minasragra, Peru, and refined a disordered monoclinic C2/m structure containing [V10O28]6- units and hydrated calcium complexes. Disorder gives the Ca1 site possible local coordination by six, seven or eight oxygen atoms, averaging seven; hydrogen positions were located in difference maps but subsequently restrained, with residual disorder and partial occupancy. The 2005 paper supports this model over its tested ordered C2 alternative; it does not provide an unconstrained determination of every local hydrogen configuration. The 1966 predecessor's publisher title specifies 16H2O whereas the 2005 reference list prints 17H2O; the current identity follows the IMA formula and inspected 2005 original. The 1966 full text remains unavailable. The inspected 2005 depository files contain thermal parameters and observed/calculated diffraction intensities, but their Table 5/6 labels differ from the article's Table 4/5 deposit references; they belong to the same experiment. Pascoite is distinct from the decavanadate ion, the broader mineral group and elemental vanadium. These structural observations establish neither microbial extraction nor isolated-product recovery or industrial deployment; criticality is not inherited from vanadium.

Pentagonite

Pentagonite is a hydrated calcium vanadyl silicate mineral, CaV4+OSi4O10(H2O)3·H2O, approved as IMA 1971-039 and retained in the September 2026 IMA list. It is a distinct mineral species from cavansite, with a six-membered-ring silicate-sheet topology and an ambient orthorhombic Ccm21 structure in the inspected primary studies. The historical Oregon description and later Wagholi studies concern different natural specimens. Laboratory heating and pressure experiments support abiotic structural changes, with protocol-dependent hydration and reversibility. These experiments do not establish a natural formation temperature, microbial activity, vanadium extraction, an isolated recovered product or industrial deployment. No criticality designation is inherited from vanadium or other constituents.

Perovskite

Perovskite is the calcium titanate mineral species with ideal formula CaTiO3. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list gives grandfathered status G and original description year 1839, not an IMA approval number. This owner identifies the mineral species, not the broader perovskite structure class, halide photovoltaic materials, elemental titanium, or a perovskite-bearing concentrate. Keller and Buseck (1994) independently characterized natural perovskite grains from Ca-Al-rich inclusions in the Allende and Vigarano carbonaceous chondrites by transmission electron microscopy and electron diffraction, using the orthorhombic Pnma setting. Their energy-dispersive analyses detected Ca and Ti without other reported detectable elements; this is detection-limited cation evidence, not proof of absolute purity or a measured oxygen balance. The paper examined over 50 grains from six extracted regions. Its separately synthesized CaTiO3 cooling experiments are not natural-feed extraction or recovery studies. Twinning observations and inferred meteorite thermal histories are kept distinct; no universal high-temperature transition sequence or cooling-rate thermometer is asserted here. No microbial mechanism, processing performance, industrial deployment or criticality designation is inferred.

Pertlikite

Pertlikite is an approved tetragonal mineral of the voltaite group, IMA 2005-055, represented in the September 2026 IMA list as K2(Fe(II),Mg)2(Mg,Fe(III))4Fe(III)2Al(SO4)12(H2O)18. It is distinct from cubic voltaite and magnesiovoltaite, rather than a synonym for any magnesium-bearing voltaite-group material. Ertl et al. (2008) characterized natural type material from Madeni Zakh, Iran, using portions of a single crystal for diffraction, optical examination and electron-microprobe analysis, with additional grains for bulk hydrogen analysis. Tetragonal I41/acd symmetry and unequal Fe/Mg site occupancies distinguish the studied crystal from the cubic structural model. The formula combines microprobe chemistry, fitted Mossbauer spectral areas and structure refinement; it is not a direct assay of every site or oxidation state. Spectral areas were not corrected for different recoil-free fractions. Measured water was 15.3 wt.% with estimated 10% relative uncertainty, whereas 16.73 wt.% in the composition table was estimated from the structure. Powder and single-crystal cell dimensions differ beyond their stated precision, and hydrogen positions around disordered Al-bound waters were not located. A proposed origin through pyrite decomposition is geological interpretation, not an observed reaction or microbial mechanism. No extraction, recovery yield or criticality designation is curated.

Petalite

Petalite is the lithium aluminium silicate mineral species LiAlSi4O10, listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 as grandfathered, with 1800 as the year of its original description (PDF page 170). This year is not an IMA approval-number identifier. The Handbook of Mineralogy describes monoclinic petalite occurring in granite pegmatites, where it can locally constitute lithium ore. This is geological resource context from the 2001 entry, not a claim about present production, universal ore grade or extractability. Its listed associations include spodumene and lepidolite; their occurrence together does not make those minerals or the lepidolite series synonyms for petalite. The species is distinct from elemental lithium, a bulk pegmatite feed, and a manufactured lithium product. No microbial mechanism or criticality designation is assigned here.

Petrukite

Indium- and tin-bearing copper-iron-zinc-silver sulfide mineral of the stannite group with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula (Cu,Ag)2(Fe,Zn)(Sn,In)S4 and approval number IMA 1985-052. Kissin and Owens (1989) characterized petrukite on cotype specimens (GSC 65049-65052, plus Herb claim metatypes AMNH T98797, BM 1987,94, Ecole des Mines T44352, and NMNH 163779) from three co-type localities: the Herb claim, Cassiar District, Turnagain River area, British Columbia, Canada; the Mount Pleasant mine, Charlotte County, New Brunswick, Canada; and the Ikuno mine, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan. Electron-microprobe analyses across the three localities (Table 5, p. 682) yielded a Herb claim mean empirical formula of (Cu1.85Fe0.95Zn0.24Ag0.03)Sigma3.07(Sn0.89In0.05)Sigma0.94S3.99 (0.05 apfu In), Mount Pleasant compositions with 0.02-0.04 apfu In, and Ikuno mine compositions spanning 0.07-0.21 apfu In via the coupled substitution Cu+ + Sn4+ <-> In3+ + Zn2+. Precession single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction on Herb claim, Mount Pleasant, and Ikuno grains indexed in orthorhombic space group Pmn21 (wurtzite-type superstructure, Table 7, pp. 680-683: Herb claim a = 7.6671(81), b = 6.4399(32), c = 6.2605(61) A; Ikuno a = 7.7050(27), b = 6.4462(14) [printed 6.4421(14) in text p. 680], c = 6.2757(26) A; Mount Pleasant a = 7.6858(101), b = 6.4395(60), c = 6.2947(23) A; Z = 2), where ordering of Cu, (Fe,Zn), and (Sn,In) lowers the symmetry from the hexagonal P63mc wurtzite subcell. No full atomic- coordinate refinement was performed in the 1989 study, and the compositional and structural boundary between Sn-dominant orthorhombic petrukite and indium-rich sakuraiite remained open to further single-crystal investigation. Distinct from sakuraiite, ferrokësterite, kësterite, stannite, and elemental indium or tin; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or extraction yield is asserted.

Phosphoferrite

Phosphoferrite is the ferrous phosphate mineral with ideal formula Fe2+3(PO4)2(H2O)3. The September 2026 IMA list records redefined status under the 1980 special procedure. It is distinct from the more hydrated species vivianite and ludlamite, the Mn-dominant related mineral reddingite, and ferric kryzhanovskite. The historical Hagendorf Sud specimen studied by Moore (1971) contained Mn and Ca and was not a pure synthetic Fe endmember. Laboratory heating produced a source-reported ferric crystalline product with diffraction similarities to the starting material. Later structural work by Moore, Araki and Kampf (1980) corrected substantial indexing and unit-cell errors in the earlier natural kryzhanovskite comparison; this record therefore retains the limited heating observation without treating the earlier cell dimensions, exact structural model or pure-product identity as established. These are abiotic laboratory observations, not microbial extraction or demonstrated industrial recovery. No criticality designation is inherited from iron or phosphorus.

Phosphophyllite

Phosphophyllite is a grandfathered monoclinic zinc-ferrous phosphate mineral, represented in the September 2026 IMA list as Zn2Fe(II)(PO4)2(H2O)4 with historical year 1920. It is a mineral species, distinct from elemental zinc, a zinc commodity and the related minerals hopeite and parahopeite. Hill (1977) refined the structure of a natural Potosi, Bolivia crystal in P21/c using three-dimensional X-ray data, resolving competing earlier structural models. Zinc/phosphate tetrahedral sheets are linked through Fe-bearing octahedra; the Potosi result is not a universal assay of every locality. Dunn and Norberg (1977) partially analyzed eleven Hagendorf and three Potosi specimens, finding variable Mn substitution for Fe in the Hagendorf material and very little Mn in the Potosi material. One borderline Hagendorf Mn:Fe weight ratio of 51:49 was explicitly insufficient, given analytical uncertainty, to establish a separate Mn-dominant species. Their unpublished specimen-by-specimen analytical table was not acquired. These natural-crystal studies support identity and composition variability, without establishing microbial extraction, a recovery yield or industrial deployment. No criticality designation is inherited from zinc, iron or phosphorus.

Piilonenite-(Nd)

Hydrated sodium-neodymium carbonate mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula NaNd(CO3)2(H2O)3 and a unique layered structure chemically analogous to the NaY(CO3)2·6H2O hexahydrate adamsite-(Y) and the Na3Y(CO3)3·3H2O trihydrate shomiokite-(Y). The primary description by Lykova et al. (2026) cites approval number IMA 2025-031, whereas the September 2026 IMA Master List (PDF p. 173) prints 2025-031b; both identifiers refer to the same Mont Saint-Hilaire holotype (CMNMC 93393, from 3-6 cm wide apophyses of the Poudrette pegmatite cutting a hornfels xenolith on level 8 of the Poudrette (Demix) quarry, previously conflated under provisional code UK119), and IMA:2025-031 is recorded as the canonical CURIE while retaining the 2025-031b suffix note from the master list. Electron-microprobe WDS analysis on holotype CMNMC 93393 (7 analyses, Table 1, p. 340) yielded Na2O 9.29, Y2O3 1.71, La2O3 0.93, Ce2O3 8.32, Pr2O3 2.75, Nd2O3 23.90, Sm2O3 6.85, Eu2O3 0.27, Gd2O3 3.64, Tb2O3 0.12, Dy2O3 0.90, Ho2O3 0.13, Er2O3 0.12, Tm2O3 0.07, CO2* 26.32, H2O* 16.16, total 101.48 wt%, corresponding to the empirical formula Na1.00(Nd0.48Ce0.17Sm0.13Gd0.07Pr0.06Y0.05La0.02Dy0.02)Sigma1.00(CO3)2(H2O)3 (with two Y-enriched zones reaching 18.43 wt% Y2O3 / 0.53 apfu Y), where CO2 and H2O were calculated by stoichiometry rather than directly measured because of the paucity of pure material. Synchrotron single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 298(2) K (ALS beamline 12.2.1, lambda = 0.7288 A, Table 3, p. 342) on an inversion-twinned crystal (54:46 ratio) refined in orthorhombic space group P212121 (a = 6.7914(11), b = 17.135(3), c = 6.4360(10) A, V = 749.0(2) A3, Z = 4, R1 = 0.092, wR2 = 0.106 for 1168 unique reflections with I > 2sigma(I) out of 1364 unique reflections), with isotropic displacement parameters retained for C2 and several O sites (O1, O4, O5, O6, O8, O9) and unlocated hydrogen positions. The mineral slowly dissolves in room-temperature aqueous HCl with effervescence (qualitative diagnostic observation, p. 339). Distinct from adamsite-(Y), shomiokite-(Y), and elemental neodymium; no criticality designation or microbial mechanism is asserted.

Pinnoite

Pinnoite is the magnesium hydroxyborate mineral MgB2O(OH)6 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Its grandfathered status G and year 1884 describe its nomenclatural history, not a sequential approval identifier. It is distinct from chloropinnoite, other magnesium borate species, elemental boron and the borates commodity. Frost and Xi (2014) examined natural material supplied as pinnoite from the Inder boron deposit and salt dome, Kazakhstan. Their institutional author manuscript reports Raman spectra from at least ten crystals using 633-nm excitation and nominal 2 cm-1 resolution, and diamond ATR-FTIR spectra from 128 scans at 4 cm-1 resolution. Figures 2a, 3a and 4a show prominent Raman bands at 900 and 745 cm-1 and OH-region bands at 3179, 3399, 3554 and 3579 cm-1. These are specimen-level spectroscopic observations, not extraction yields or a new chemical-purity assay. The manuscript does not establish a complete bulk composition or report a new diffraction refinement for these crystals. Interpretation is limited by internal inconsistencies: manuscript page 5 says the OH-stretching region provides no water-band evidence, whereas page 7 assigns bands at 1629, 1665 and 1696 cm-1 to water bending and considers strongly adsorbed surface water. These passages do not establish occupied structural-water sites or justify changing the accepted ideal formula. The 745 cm-1 assignment differs between the results and conclusion; the infrared 3543 cm-1 value in the results differs from 3513 cm-1 in Figure 4b, abstract and conclusion. Hydrogen-bond distances are estimates from an empirical spectral correlation, not directly measured interatomic distances. Proposed nanomaterial uses were not tested as material performance. This characterization does not establish a microbial mechanism, recovered boron product, industrial deployment or jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Polylithionite

Polylithionite is the lithium-bearing mica mineral species listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with formula KLi2AlSi4O10F2 and approved status (PDF page 175). Its 1998 s.p. entry denotes a special-procedure action, not a modern approval-number CURIE. The Handbook of Mineralogy describes monoclinic material and uses the generalized formula KLi2AlSi4O10(F,OH)2; its natural specimen analyses and hydroxyl substitution are not substituted for the current IMA formula. Documented geological occurrence includes late-stage segregations, veinlets and metasomatic replacement in syenite pegmatites of the Lovozero alkalic massif. This establishes a lithium-bearing geological host, not a universal ore grade, present mining status or recovery process. The IMA-approved mica nomenclature report defines lepidolite as a series name for trioctahedral micas on or near the trilithionite-polylithionite join. Lepidolite is therefore not used as an exact synonym for this endmember; a lepidolite-labelled mixed feed needs specimen-specific characterization before its behavior can be assigned to polylithionite. This species is distinct from elemental lithium and a bulk lithium concentrate. No microbial mechanism or criticality designation is assigned here.

Powellite

Powellite is the calcium molybdate mineral species Ca(MoO4), listed as grandfathered in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. It is distinct from elemental molybdenum, wulfenite and an uncharacterized calcium molybdate precipitate. Sidorenko and colleagues (2008) examined black Ca-Mo-rich grains from the Bota-Burum Mo-U deposit, South Kazakhstan. Powder diffraction and infrared spectroscopy supported crystalline powellite in the uranophane-beta-associated material. Chemically similar grains from the uramarsite-associated material were optically isotropic and X-ray amorphous, with no characteristic powellite infrared bands; the authors interpreted these as metamict powellite. That interpretation is kept distinct from the directly characterized crystalline material. Radiation-induced alteration and the origin of the black colour were inferred, without a controlled irradiation test. The article's page 29 discussion is internally inconsistent about retention versus loss of anisotropy and diffraction in the silicate assemblage; the explicit characterization on pages 23-27 anchors this limited record. These observations establish neither a microbial transformation nor a mineral recovery yield. Criticality is unrecorded.

Preobrazhenskite

Preobrazhenskite is the grandfathered magnesium borate species Mg3B11O15(OH)9 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Its 1956 entry is an original-description year, not an approval identifier. Burns and Hawthorne refined a natural crystal from the Inder borate deposit, Kazakhstan, in orthorhombic Pbcn symmetry, with a = 16.291(4), b = 9.181(2) and c = 10.571(2) angstrom. Complex borate sheets parallel to (010) are linked through two octahedrally coordinated magnesium sites. Hydrogen positions were located from difference-Fourier maps; a crystallographically symmetric H site is an average structural model whose true local symmetry the authors explicitly left uncertain. Possible off-centre disorder and a high-temperature transition were suggestions, not experimentally demonstrated transformations. The study reported no new bulk chemical analysis or microbial experiment. This magnesium borate is distinct from potassium-bearing kaliborite, elemental boron and the borates commodity. No criticality designation, extraction mechanism or industrial recovery is inferred.

Priceite

Priceite is the Ca2B5O7(OH)5(H2O) mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with grandfathered status G and original- description year 1873, not an approval number. Pandermite is a historical name for the same species. It is distinct from colemanite, gowerite, elemental boron and the borates commodity. Wallwork et al. determined a monoclinic P21/c structure from synchrotron powder diffraction of natural Sultancayir material, South Australian Museum specimen G3769. The model has four tetrahedral and one triangular boron sites per formula unit; boron positions were assigned geometrically and not refined, and hydrogen positions were not located. Hydroxyl and water assignments were supported by bond-valence analysis. The paper's abstract and body disagree on the borate-chain direction, so no direction is selected here. A separate Fuka, Japan, study reports eight electron-probe analyses averaging 49.95 wt% B2O3 and 32.35 wt% CaO. Its 17.56 wt% H2O was calculated by difference because pure material was insufficient for direct determination; its 2.486 g/cm3 density was calculated, not measured. The proposed natural alteration of shimazakiite and its inferred temperature range are geological interpretations, not a controlled synthesis experiment. No criticality, microbial mechanism or industrial extraction performance is inferred from these observations.

Probertite

Probertite is the NaCaB5O7(OH)4(H2O)3 mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1929, not a sequential approval identifier. It is distinct from ulexite, elemental boron, the borates commodity and mixed ores containing probertite. Gatta et al. studied natural Kramer Deposit material from collection specimen 11717, using separate crystals for X-ray diffraction at 293 K and neutron diffraction at 20 K. Both refinements used monoclinic P21/c; the model contains pentaborate chains with three tetrahedral and two triangular boron sites, four hydroxyl groups and three water molecules per formula unit. Ten hydrogen sites were first located using neutron data and then incorporated into the X-ray refinement. Chemical analyses are specimen-specific: electron-probe results give CaO 15.8(2) and Na2O 8.6(3) wt%, while the separate trace-element table reports a mean lithium concentration of 0.392 wt ppm from ten analyses. Near-ideal major-cation composition does not mean zero trace elements or establish purity for every deposit. The paper reports limitations of its neutron extinction correction; the deposited CIFs and final publisher version were not acquired. This identity and characterization record makes no criticality, microbial extraction, isolated-product recovery or demonstrated radiation-shielding deployment claim.

Regerite

Regerite is a hydrated potassium ferric phosphate mineral with ideal formula KFe6(PO4)4(OH)7(H2O)6·4H2O, approved as IMA 2023-028 and retained in the September 2026 IMA list. Rewitzer et al. (2023) characterized crystals from a historical Kreuzberg pegmatite specimen from Pleystein, Germany. The natural material contains titanium; wavelength-dispersive analyses of 15 crystals are not independent occurrences or a synthesis experiment. Water was calculated from the structural model and an assumed charge-compensating substitution, rather than directly measured. Single-crystal synchrotron diffraction at 100 K supports monoclinic P21/c symmetry and a framework of iron-centred octahedra and phosphate tetrahedra with potassium and water in channels. Bond-valence sums support the ferric assignment, rather than a separate direct iron-valence assay. Twenty-five of the 27 ideal hydrogen positions were located and refined with restraints; H22 and H30b remained unresolved. The deposited all-Fe model and ideal formula do not represent the full measured titanium-bearing composition. The proposed titanium distribution, displacement and charge-compensation scheme remain interpretations, with displaced Ti not unambiguously confirmed. The text's O18-to-O33 water-site range overlaps its hydroxyl assignment; Table 4 and the deposited hydrogen model instead distinguish O17-to-O23 hydroxyl sites from O24-to-O33 water sites. Natural occurrence and crystal structure do not establish a formation, microbial extraction or recovery mechanism. No criticality designation is inherited from constituent elements.

Renierite

Renierite is the mineral species listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with formula (Cu1+,Zn)11Fe4(Ge4+,As5+)2S16 and renamed status, 2007 s.p. The special-procedure date is not an IMA approval-number identifier. The older Handbook uses the spelling Renierite with an acute accent on the second e and describes a tetragonal, pseudocubic sulfide occurring in germanium-bearing hydrothermal polymetallic deposits, including Kipushi and Tsumeb. Bernstein's 1986 electron-microprobe study supports coupled compositional variation between zincian Cu10ZnGe2Fe4S16 and arsenian Cu11GeAsFe4S16 within renierite; these compositional endmembers are not assigned separate accepted-species records here. Table 3 combines newly measured analyses, earlier literature values and ideal formulas, and Figure 4 distinguishes those origins. Microscopy shows intergrowths with other sulfides, including germanite, rather than identical material identity. This record concerns the mineral, not a bulk copper ore, germanium element or a traded metal. No microbial extraction mechanism, isolated recovery yield, present production or inherited criticality is asserted from these mineralogical observations.

Rhabdophane-(Ce)

Rhabdophane-(Ce) is the cerium-dominant hydrated phosphate mineral listed by IMA-CNMNC with ideal formula Ce(PO4)·H2O and renamed status Rn, 1966 s.p., in September 2026. That nomenclature entry is not a numbered approval identifier. It is distinct from elemental cerium, an unspecified mixed rare-earth phosphate and anhydrous monazite-(Ce). Synthetic Ce-rich rhabdophane prepared by replacement of Durango fluorapatite was identified by powder diffraction and thermal characterization in Bamforth et al. (2024). The fitted monoclinic structural model is study-specific; the Sm reference structure used in refinement is not a Ce-specimen accession. Ideal hydration is not an assay of every synthetic powder: Shelyug et al. (2018) reported CePO4·0.732H2O from thermogravimetry including adsorbed and structural water. Porous monazite and rhabdophane can have overlapping low electron-microprobe totals, so elemental composition or totals alone do not distinguish these phases. The curated transformation is an abiotic laboratory result. No microbial mechanism, isolated cerium recovery, industrial deployment or inherited criticality is asserted.

Rhabdophane-(La)

Rhabdophane-(La) is the lanthanum-dominant hydrated phosphate mineral listed by IMA-CNMNC with ideal formula La(PO4)·H2O and renamed status Rn, 1987 s.p., in September 2026. This entry does not provide a numbered IMA approval identifier. It is distinct from elemental lanthanum, mixed rare-earth phosphate material, rhabdophane-(Ce) and anhydrous monazite-(La). Ondrejka et al. (2018) characterized natural La-dominant members within mixed, compositionally zoned rhabdophane-group grains from the Velence Hills, Hungary, using electron microprobe and Raman spectroscopy. Their analyses include substitutions and mixed end-member contributions; neither every grain nor every La-Nd-rich zone is pure rhabdophane-(La). Natural-grain hydration is not measured by oxide totals alone. The 2019 erratum requires inclusion of Fe in formula calculations without recognizing an Fe end-member. Shelyug et al. (2018) separately characterized synthetic La rhabdophane and its thermal conversion to monazite. Their fitted monoclinic model and total-water coefficient 0.804 describe that preparation, not a universal species assay or revised IMA formula. No microbial mechanism, isolated lanthanum recovery, industrial deployment or inherited criticality designation is curated.

Richetite

Grandfathered hydrated lead-iron-magnesium uranyl oxide hydroxide mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula (Fe3+,Mg)xPb2+8.6(UO2)36O36(OH)24(H2O)41, status G, and original-description year 1947 (not a numbered IMA approval CURIE). Originally described by Vaes (1947) from the Shinkolobwe mine, Katanga (Haut-Katanga), Democratic Republic of the Congo, richetite was structurally solved for the first time by Burns (1998) on a Shinkolobwe crystal provided by William Pinch. Electron-microprobe WDS analysis (5 points, Table 2, p. 188) detected UO3 (77.02-77.83 wt%, mean 77.43 wt%) and PbO (16.76-17.37 wt%, mean 17.06 wt%), corresponding to a U:Pb atomic ratio of 1:0.282 (10.15 Pb2+ per 36 U), whereas Fe and Mg were below the microprobe detection limit on that thin flake (~0.25 wt% FeO/MgO inferred from structure). Single-crystal SMART CCD X-ray diffraction refined in triclinic space group P1 (a = 20.9391(3), b = 12.1000(2), c = 16.3450(3) A, alpha = 103.87(1), beta = 115.37(1), gamma = 90.27(1) degrees, V = 3605.2 A3, Z = 1, R = 8.9%, S = 1.79 for 12,383 unique observed reflections with |Fo| > 4sigma_F; attempts to refine in P-1 failed) established alpha-U3O8-type uranyl oxide hydroxy-hydrate sheets [(UO2)18O18(OH)12] stacked with 13 partially occupied interlayer Pb2+ sites (8.74 Pb pfu), two octahedral M(1)/M(2) sites (modeled with 0.47(5) Fe2+ + 0.53(5) Mg2+ at M(1) and 0.30(5) Mg2+ at M(2), x = 1.30), and 41 H2O sites, yielding the 1998 structural formula MxPb8.74[(UO2)18O18(OH)12]2(H2O)41. Hydrogen positions were not directly refined, and only U and Pb atoms were modeled anisotropically. The subsequent 2017 refinement cited in the IMA Master List (American Mineralogist 102 (2017), 1771, specifying (Fe3+,Mg)x and Pb2+8.6) is behind a paywall and was not independently acquired at curation. Distinct from masuyite, fourmarierite, vandendriesscheite, curite, and elemental uranium or lead; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or extraction yield is asserted.

Rivadavite

Rivadavite is the approved sodium-magnesium borate mineral Na6Mg[B6O7(OH)6]4·10H2O, IMA1966-010, in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Hurlbut and Aristarain's 1967 original study described natural nodular crystal aggregates embedded in borax at Tincalayu, Argentina, with wet chemistry, morphology and diffraction evidence. Its historical Na6MgB24O40·22H2O formula expresses the same total elemental inventory as the current formula, but does not resolve the modern OH/water partition. The authors distinguished measured density 1.905(2) g/cm3 from calculated density 1.910 g/cm3 and reported P21/m from diffraction, etching and negative pyroelectric tests. Their unexplained small extinction angle remained a qualification. The later 1973 atomic-structure note was verified at the publisher only as metadata; its full text was not acquired, so no atomic model or revised lattice parameters are adopted from it. This species is distinct from associated borax, kernite, elemental boron and the borates commodity; criticality, microbial activity and industrial recovery are not inferred.

Romanèchite

Romanèchite is a barium-bearing manganese oxide mineral with the IMA formula (Ba,H2O)2(Mn4+,Mn3+)5O10. The September 2026 list marks it approved (A), with "1982 s.p." in the number/year column; special-procedure notation is not a YYYY-NNN accession. The Handbook describes its monoclinic crystal structure. Romanèchite is a mineral species, distinct from barium or manganese elements, cryptomelane, and mixed manganese ores. The historical collective term psilomelane is not treated as an exact synonym for a pure mineral species. No constituent commodity's criticality is inherited. Pracejus's September 1989 thesis supplies mixed-ore experimental context rather than an accepted romanèchite-specific microbial mechanism. Section 5.5 correlates calculated normative mineral proportions of Groote Eylandt cemented pisolites with results from an Enterobacter-species leaching series. Appendix I.3.2 describes 1.89 g heat-sterilized ore, 8 mL 1% w/v molasses, incubation at 32 degrees C, and weekly concentrated H2SO4 addition before centrifugation and supernatant AAS, followed by fresh molasses and bacteria for a 21-week series. The normative romanèchite calculation allocates barium to this phase and neglects its variable potassium, intergrowths and other potential hosts; it is not a direct time-resolved phase abundance measurement. Figures 5.12-5.13 therefore cannot establish a pure-romanèchite bacterial dissolution yield. Matched uninoculated and acid-only results are not presented in the inspected leaching methods, figures or Appendix V.2. The record retains this experimental relevance without assigning a species/strain CURIE, microbial necessity, mineral-specific rate, isolated recovery, or industrial use.

Roquesite

Roquesite is the copper-indium sulfide mineral species CuInS2, listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with renamed status (Rn) and IMA number 1962-001. Picot and Pierrot's original description concerns natural material from Charrier, Allier, France, observed as inclusions in bornite. Powder diffraction, reflected-light microscopy and electron-microprobe observations support its distinction from the associated host minerals. The paper compares this natural material with a separately supplied synthetic CuInS2 specimen; that comparator is not the natural mineral specimen or a microbial product. The synthetic powder pattern contains additional broad central lines whose origin the authors could not test because material was scarce. The natural specimen has reported traces of iron and zinc, so qualitative element-map contrast is not evidence of absolute chemical purity. Both natural and synthetic microprobe analyses total above 100 percent; the authors attribute the excess mainly to sulfur-standard and correction difficulties and also discuss possible reference-metal surface oxidation. Those analyses support the mineral assignment without establishing a closed recovery balance. This record identifies the mineral species, not elemental indium, the entire polymetallic ore or every manufactured material of nominal CuInS2 composition. No microbial mechanism, isolated-metal yield, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality is asserted.

Roscoelite

Roscoelite is a vanadium-bearing mica mineral with the ideal formula KV3+2(Si3Al)O10(OH)2 in the September 2026 IMA list. The list records status A and the special-procedure entry 1998 s.p.; that entry is not an original discovery year or a conventional numbered approval. Blake's 1876 description concerns natural mica from Granite Creek, El Dorado County, California, and explicitly corrects his initial chromium identification to vanadium. The species is distinct from vanadium as an element, generic vanadium-bearing mica, and mixed shale or ore feeds. Ito's synthetic material was assigned to roscoelite by powder diffraction indexed as a 1M mica; its mixed-valence, nonideal bulk chemistry and microscopic oxide inclusions must not be replaced by the ideal all-V3+ formula. No criticality designation is inherited from vanadium, and neither the natural occurrence nor abiotic synthesis establishes microbial extraction or industrial recovery.

Sakuraiite

Indium-dominant copper-zinc-iron-indium-tin sulfide mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula (Cu,Zn,Fe)3(In,Sn)S4 and approval number IMA 1965-017. Originally described by Kato (1965) from the Kanagase vein group of the Ikuno mine, Asago-cho, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan, with a tetragonal or pseudotetragonal subcell (a = 5.455, c = 10.91 A, Z = 2) and an Ag-rich formula (Cu,Zn,Fe,Ag)3(In,Sn)S4, type material from the Ikuno mine (including Kato's 1965 holotype and specimen NSM M-15843 from the Senju-hon vein) was chemically re-examined by Shimizu, Kato, and Shiozawa (1986). Electron-microprobe analyses (Table 1: 5 sakuraiite analyses SK 1-5, 3 coexisting indium-bearing stannite/petrukite analyses ST 1-3, and 2 indium- bearing kësterite analyses KS 1-2, plus step-scan traverses across zoned grains in Figure 3) showed that Kato's 1965 elevated Ag values (3.5-4 wt%) were erroneous (actual Ag 0.10-0.15 wt% in sakuraiite) and established the revised formula (Cu,Zn,Fe)3(In,Sn)S4 with In:Sn atomic ratios reaching 89:11 (analysis SK 2: Cu 1.221, Ag 0.004, Fe 0.436, Zn 1.302, Mn 0.001, Cd 0.032, Sn 0.189, In 0.817, S 3.987 on an 8-atom basis) via coupled (Zn,Fe)In-for-CuSn substitution toward a hypothetical (Zn,Fe)2CuInS4 end-member. Shimizu et al. (1986) did not report new X-ray diffraction measurements, and Kissin and Owens (1989, pp. 684-686) subsequently examined Ikuno mine specimens, identified orthorhombic Pmn21 petrukite and an unindexed Zn > Fe phase, and noted that holotype sakuraiite still required definitive X-ray diffraction characterization to resolve its crystal symmetry and structural relationship to petrukite. Distinct from petrukite, roquesite, stannite, kësterite, and elemental indium or tin; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or extraction yield is asserted.

Saléeite

Saléeite is the magnesium uranyl phosphate decahydrate mineral Mg(UO2)2(PO4)2(H2O)10 in the September 2026 IMA list, with grandfathered status G. The year 1932 denotes its original description, not a numbered IMA approval. It is distinct from lower-hydration metasaléeite, arsenate-bearing nováčekite, aluminium-bearing sabugalite, and elemental magnesium or uranium. Dal Bo and colleagues examined natural saléeite from Shinkolobwe, Democratic Republic of Congo, with associated torbernite. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 293(2) K supports a monoclinic P21/n structure with uranyl-phosphate sheets and hydrated interlayer magnesium. The refined saléeite cell is a = 6.9516(3), b = 19.942(1), c = 6.9667(3) angstrom and beta = 90.586(4) degrees; R1 is 0.0307 for 1990 observed reflections after the reported twin treatment. Qualitative EDS detected U, P, Mg and O but no Fe or As, whereas the crystallographic occupancy model refined 0.97(1) Mg and 0.03(1) Fe at the interlayer cation site. These are different analytical results, not proof of a chemically pure endmember. Hydrogen positions used restrained O-H distances and constrained displacement parameters. This identity and structure evidence does not establish a microbial transformation, an extraction yield, an industrial process or a universal dehydration threshold. No criticality claim is inferred from the mineral's constituents. Deposited reflection data CSD-430599 were not acquired or independently re-refined, and the separate bassetite oxidation discussion is not a saléeite experiment.

Černý and colleagues (2001) characterized natural zincian stannite and ferroan kësterite from four Peerless pegmatite nodules using electron microprobe analyses and powder-diffraction unit-cell refinement. They explicitly named the samples by composition; their work does not refine cation ordering or establish every specimen's space group. Haase and colleagues (2022) independently identified stannite by selected-area electron diffraction in selected natural grains from two Czech mine-waste sites. Their weathering textures and compositional series do not establish microbial causation or a recovery process. The laboratory leaching evidence below concerns separately prepared synthetic material and one historically identified Malaysian natural sample. No criticality designation is inherited from tin, copper or zinc.

Stolzite

Stolzite is the lead tungstate mineral species Pb(WO4), listed as grandfathered in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. It is distinct from elemental tungsten, wulfenite and a mixed lead-tungsten ore. Kiseleva and colleagues (2008, pages 18-21 and Figures 3-4) describe natural Mo-bearing stolzite from the Bugdaya deposit, eastern Transbaikalia, Russia. Electron-microprobe composition was reported as Pb(W0.74Mo0.26)O4; this is a W-dominant solid-solution composition, not a pure PbWO4 analysis or a distinct species named chillagite. The grains occupy fractures and cavities in galena and occur with anglesite and covellite. Small grains prevented crystal-structure investigation, so the source's assignment is retained with that limitation. Its proposed supergene origin is an interpretation of mineral associations, not a demonstrated reaction pathway. The occurrence does not establish extractable reserves or recovery yield. Microbial mechanisms and criticality designations are unrecorded.

Sulfoborite

Sulfoborite is a grandfathered magnesium borate-sulfate mineral listed as Mg3[B(OH)4]2(SO4)(OH,F)2 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. The list's 1893 entry is a description year, not an approval identifier. Giese and Penna's 1983 single-crystal X-ray study of a natural Westeregeln specimen produced an orthorhombic Pnma structural model with octahedral magnesium, tetrahedral boron and sulfur, hydroxyl groups and a separate fluorine site. Their ideal Mg3[B(OH)4]2(SO4)(OH)F formula and absence of molecular water are conclusions from that structure; they did not chemically analyze the measured crystal. The current species formula's variable OH/F notation is retained rather than replaced with a universally fixed composition. Detailed hydrogen-bond assignments remain qualified by a later neutron study whose complete original was not accessible in this session. This identity record asserts no extraction, transformation or recovery mechanism, industrial deployment or criticality designation. The mineral is distinct from elemental boron, magnesium metal and bulk borate commodities.

Svanbergite

Svanbergite is the strontium aluminium sulfate-phosphate mineral SrAl3(SO4)(PO4)(OH)6, distinct from calcium-dominant woodhouseite, strontium aluminium phosphate goyazite and strontium as an element. The September 2026 IMA list records its redefinition by special procedure in 1987. Kato and Miura (1977) refined a natural crystal from Dover Andalusite Mine, Nevada, British Museum specimen BM 17702. Single-crystal diffraction used 283 reflections and supported R-3m symmetry, a=6.992(2) and c=16.567(5) angstrom, with R=0.085. This specimen-specific structure contains disordered phosphorus/sulfur tetrahedral sites; the paper does not provide a new chemical analysis of that exact crystal or locate all hydrogen atoms directly. Its separate jarosite specimen and comparisons with earlier structures are not svanbergite synthesis experiments. Stoffregen and Alpers (1987) measured variable natural aluminium phosphate-sulfate grains in three hydrothermal ore deposits. Svanbergite-rich grains accompany alunite or kaolinite in shallower Summitville material, while La Escondida includes intermediate Ca/Sr compositions assigned probable hypogene or supergene origins from textures. Figure 1 shows a grain with subequal Ca and Sr rather than a pure svanbergite endmember; Table 3 and Figure 2 retain compositional variation and calculated water. Replacement or dissolution of apatite in acidic, sulfate-rich alteration is a geological interpretation, not a time-resolved transformation assay or demonstrated microbial mechanism. The 250 degrees C stability diagram in Figure 3 is a calcium-system woodhouseite inference and must not be treated as an experimentally measured svanbergite stability field. The companion woodhouseite record uses the same field-study lineage. Mineral identity and qualified natural alteration context are supported; microbial formation, strontium recovery yield, industrial deployment and mineral-specific criticality are not asserted.

Synchysite-(Ce)

A calcium-cerium fluorcarbonate mineral with the ideal IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula CaCe(CO3)2F. The authority lists renamed status and identifier 1982-030; these identify this species, not the Nd- or Y-dominant synchysite species, bastnäsite, a rare-earth element or a mixed ore concentrate. Conconi et al. (2025) examined five natural crystals from miarolitic cavities in the Cuasso al Monte granophyre, Italy. Four crystals (FCBN1–FCBN4) supplied monoclinic C2/c average-structure refinements; Raman and SEM–EDS characterization used a subset, and TEM–EDS/electron diffraction used two lamellae from the separate FCBN5 crystal, as specified in Table A1. The crystals show chemical zoning, stacking disorder and inclusions. For FCBN3, Table 3 reports mean Ce contents of 0.44 atoms per formula unit in the core (13 spots) and 0.30 in the outer rim (11 spots), normalized to two cations; these are local composition averages, not recovery measurements or a uniform species formula. Low measured fluorine may reflect beam-induced loss. Fictitious scattering-site occupancies and calculated densities from the diffraction refinements do not directly represent measured chemistry. The proposed screw-dislocation growth sequence and Th-related loss of crystallinity are interpretations of natural microstructure; beam damage and other defects limit causal attribution. No controlled microbial, extraction, or recovery experiment is curated here. Underlying FCF diffraction files were available only upon request and were not acquired; published tables and Appendix A were inspected. No criticality designation is transferred from contained rare-earth elements.

Tennantite-(In)

Tennantite-(In) is the approved tetrahedrite-group mineral species with ideal formula Cu6(Cu5In)As4S13 and IMA number 2023-011. It is distinct from elemental indium, other members of the tennantite series and the entire polymetallic ore. Voudouris and colleagues describe natural anhedral grains from the Pefka epithermal deposit in Greece, associated with roquesite, galena and tennantite-(Fe) in quartz. Their study reuses the sample investigated by Voudouris and colleagues in 2022, rather than establishing an independent occurrence. Backscattered-electron imaging, wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analyses and single-crystal X-ray diffraction support the mineral assignment. The seven selected chemical spot analyses near the extracted crystal are part of 86 analyses of the zoned specimen, not seven independent deposits or a bulk ore grade. The refined structural model supports indium at the tetrahedrally coordinated M(1) site; its formal trivalent state is interpreted from chemical and structural constraints rather than measured by a separate valence-sensitive assay. The natural compositions include substitutions and do not equal the ideal end-member formula. Possible intergrowths with lead-bearing phases limit interpretation of minor lead as lattice substitution. The reported powder diffraction pattern and density are calculated; powder diffraction and hardness were not measured on this scarce material. The proposed crystallization sequence and changing fluid conditions are geological interpretations, not controlled reaction experiments. Abstract and Table 3 uncertainties for lead and arsenic differ, so those conflicting uncertainties are not adopted as precise measurements here. No microbial mechanism, extraction yield, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality is assigned.
